title: The Lion's Whisker
text:
An Ethiopian folk tale tells of a woman who married a widower with a young son. The boy grieved for his mother and would have nothing to do with his stepmother. He refused the food she cooked and turned away from her kindness. In despair, she went to a wise old man and asked him for a potion that would make the boy love her.

He said he could make one, but he needed a whisker from a living lion. The woman was terrified, but she wanted the boy's love badly enough to try.

She took meat out to where a lion lived and left it at a distance, then retreated. Day after day she returned, each time coming a little closer and staying a little longer. The lion grew used to her. In time it ate from near her feet, and finally it let her sit beside it. One day, as it lay quietly, she reached out and plucked a single whisker.

She ran with it to the wise man. He took it, looked at it, and threw it into the fire. She cried out in dismay. He told her she did not need a potion. She had approached a wild lion with patience, little by little, until it trusted her. If she approached the boy the same way, he too would come to her.
lesson: Trust from a hurt child cannot be forced or bought. It is won the slow way: small, steady steps, repeated until they are believed.
people: A stepmother, her stepson, a wise man, a lion
source: Ethiopian folktale; retold in Brent Ashabranner and Russell Davis, The Lion's Whisker: Tales of High Africa (1959)
caveat: Versions differ in details, and in some the woman is trying to win back a husband rather than a stepson.
